analysis.title: Capital... Costs!
key_insights: Citadel Securities head of Fixed Income Nohshad Shah attributes the global rise in yields to three pillars: a continued case for tighter policy (fiscal largesse, resilient labour markets, an energy shock on top of several years of above-target inflation), an upgraded market view of real growth and the real rates the economy can absorb, and the AI-investment cycle becoming a larger claim on capital markets.

Risk assets have held up despite additional tightening being priced. The author reads this as markets not treating higher policy rates as an automatic recession signal. US forward rates such as 5y5y have participated in the sell-off, so the front end is not doing all the work.

About $500bn of AI-related debt has been issued, and hyperscalers account for less than half. Financing also runs through datacentre project finance and private credit, for example Apollo's $35bn private financing commitment for Broadcom's AI platform.

High-quality, long-dated AI-related debt supply is an increasingly substantial alternative to sovereign duration. The author sees this competition as an additional headwind for government bonds even where the growth and inflation outlook has changed little.
The AI boom that supports risk assets is also raising the yield governments must pay to compete for capital.
Europe has less of the AI-investment offset than the US, which the author says risks importing more of the costs of the boom without the benefits.

French 10y yields are up roughly 130bp since end-2025, likely adding about €4.5bn (~15bp of GDP) to national interest expense. France carries debt of 119% of GDP, and the Banque de France expects 0.4% real growth this year.

Marine Le Pen's €140bn savings target by 2032, including a return to primary balance within 18 months of taking office, would be a 3.85% of projected GDP swing in the primary balance. That implies a primary surplus France has not achieved since the early 2000s, and the credibility of the savings is contested.

When the effective interest rate exceeds nominal growth (r–g), stabilising debt/GDP requires a primary surplus. Higher yields feed in progressively as debt refinances, and weak growth leaves more of the adjustment to fiscal policy.

The US has more room: nominal growth of 5–6% versus a reported average borrowing cost of ~3.5%, plus reserve-currency status and Treasury market depth. The author says this buys time, not immunity, because large enough primary deficits can overwhelm favourable r–g.
The author expects market pressure to stay most acute where high debt meets weak nominal growth, with promises of consolidation that the politics cannot deliver.

tension_points.theme: AI boom and government bond yields
tension_points.bull_case: The AI-investment cycle helps the US economy absorb higher rates, and risk assets are holding up despite additional tightening being priced.
tension_points.bear_case: The same boom raises yields governments must pay to compete for capital. About $500bn of AI-related debt, much of it high-quality and long-dated, is an alternative to sovereign duration.

tension_points.bull_case: Le Pen's €140bn savings target by 2032, with a return to primary balance within 18 months, is ambitious on paper.
tension_points.bear_case: The proposed savings are contested, and the 3.85% of GDP primary balance swing implies a surplus not seen since the early 2000s, while real growth is only 0.4% and debt is 119% of GDP.
